utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the people in the courtroom assisting us. For the purpose of the transcript, I know that Mr. Pusic is not here today. Today we will hear the Prosecution who will reply to the 98 bis procedure. That said, last week it was the Defence that held the floor. I can see that Mr. Scott is ready. He's got the lectern in front of him, so I shall give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and to all those in and around the courtroom. May it please the Court, before addressing the Defence submissions in particular the Prosecution will briefly address the standard of course to be used by the Pre-Trial Chamber in its application of Rule 98 bis to the evidence that has been presented by the Prosecution during its case in chief. The current version of Rule 98 bis, which everyone knows by now focuses on counts rather than charges or offences has been applied in several cases and most recently in the Milutinovic case in May of 2007. Rule 98 bis provides: "At the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable to support -- capable of supporting a conviction." Of course that Rule is to be applied separately to each of the accused who made a Rule 98 bis submission. The Prosecution submits that the Milutinovic Trial Chamber correctly set out the test to be applied, and that is: "The test to be applied is whether there is evidence upon which, if accepted, a Tribunal of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of a particular accused on the count in question. The test is not whether a Trial Chamber would in fact convict beyond a reasonable doubt but, rather, whether it could do so." And that's from the Milutinovic ruling on the 18th of May, 2007. That Trial Chamber went on to say that in applying Rule 98 bis, the Trial Chamber does not engage in an assessment of the credibility of witnesses unless, unless, such evidence is "so incapable of belief that it could not properly support a conviction even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution." The Prosecution, Your Honours, respectfully submits that no evidence tendered by the Prosecution falls into that category, that is any evidence that would be considered "incapable of belief." However, in the alternative, even if the Chamber were to find some piece of evidence that it considers to fall in that category, if there is any such evidence in the Prosecution case it is certainly extremely limited and so limited by its extent and nature as to have no significant bearing on the totality of the Prosecution's case. Further, except perhaps again in the most extreme cases, the Rule 98 bis process does not involve weighing the evidence, that is, balancing the Prosecution evidence against any evidence that the Defence might have introduced through the cross-examination of witnesses. This is not the time when the Chamber takes the Prosecution case on the one hand of evidence and Defence evidence on the other hand and weighs and balances it out. That is not the function or process under Rule 98 bis. And finally again, the Rule does not require that the Chamber be satisfied that there be evidence supporting each of the individual charges making up a count as we have discussed in this case over the last few weeks. The Trial Chamber's application of Rule 98 bis is concerned with counts only, even when those counts are themselves comprised of different crime bases or modes of liability. Moreover, as set out in paragraphs 221 to 228 of the amended indictment, these accused are charged with more than one mode of criminal liability. The Prosecution respectfully submits that the testimonial and documentary evidence adduced in its case in chief compellingly establishes the criminal responsibility of each accused as to each count charged in the amended indictment. That is that a broad range of crimes were committed throughout the territory of the so-called Herceg-Bosna during 1992 and 1993; that these crimes were directed against the Bosnian Muslim population as part of a deliberate, widespread and systematic campaign; that the objective of this campaign was to subjugate, remove and ethnically cleanse Bosnian Muslims and others of non-Croat nationality from the territory claimed to comprise Herceg-Bosna; and that most importantly each of the accused bears individual criminal liability for these crimes. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution does not intend to engage in a lengthy and detailed recitation of the evidence proving the many crimes that were committed repeatedly, time after time, starting primarily in October 1992 in Prozor and continuing until late 1993 and even into the early part of 1994. The methods and means used to achieve the removal of the Muslim population remain consistent throughout this time whether by murder, imprisonment, deportation, destruction, or plunder, the only change that occurs over the period of time is the scale and ferocity with which these crimes were carried out. Mr. President, Your Honours, as we understand them, the accused who have made submissions have essentially, essentially not challenged for purposes of Rule 98 bis we understand that they do not admit or agree to the facts generally or for purposes of ultimate judgement, that we understand the submissions to generally not question the fact of the crime base other than general statements. For example, as I understand the essence of the Coric argument on rapes, the Defence is not really arguing that rapes did not occur but denies Coric's responsibility for them on one basis or another. For example, they were not reported, I think I heard last week there was nothing that could be done or what could be done had been done, et cetera, but not that the rapes did not occur. And I submit, Your Honour, Prosecution submits, that on the basis of the Defence submissions that were made last week, what we call the crime base, if you will, has generally not been questioned. And for that reason, largely for that reason, the Prosecution will not address at any length or detail the particular crime base evidence in the case except as it relates to particular issues that have been raised by those accused who have made submissions. Nor will we address anything like all of what might be called the linkage, "linkage" evidence as to each accused who has made a 98 bis submission and nor will we address all of the forms or theories of liability. For Rule 98 bis purposes, the only question is whether each count survives as to each accused on some theory or basis of liability. For this purpose, for 98 bis purposes, the Prosecution will focus our analysis and submissions primarily on the existence and operation of a joint criminal enterprise in forms 1 and 3. We will not, for example, be addressing the liability of any accused under Article 7(3), because we submit that the Chamber need not reach or need not consider this basis in order to determine that each count survives as to each accused. The Prosecution's submissions, subject of course to the Chamber's guidance will proceed as follows: First in just a moment, the Prosecution will briefly touch on the joint criminal enterprise language from some Tribunal cases so that the Chamber might have that jurisprudence and language in mind in considering the Prosecution's further submissions. Second, we will present to you at some length an overview of the case, its principal features, and operation of the joint criminal enterprise. Again this will not involve a detailed consideration of the crime base evidence but will provide, and again at some length, an overall review of the Prosecution case. Following that overall submission, the Prosecution will then deal with the particular submissions by the Petkovic, the Coric, and the Pusic Defence teams. As to some Tribunal jurisprudence and language concerning the joint criminal enterprise, we would note this from the Krajisnik case: There the Trial Chamber found that the central purpose of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and the Chamber may want to consider whether and to what extent this parallels the purposes and objectives of the Bosnian Croat leadership, but in the Krajisnik case concerning the Bosnian Serb leadership, the Chamber found that the central purpose was: "To ethnically recompose the territories under its control by expelling and thereby drastically reducing the proportion of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats living there." It found that the crimes of deportation and forced transfer "were necessary means of implementing the common objective of removal by force of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from large areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina" and referred to these crimes as "original crimes" which fit under what we might call joint criminal enterprise form 1. That's the Krajisnik trial judgement, paragraph 1097. Beyond these crimes the indictment in the Krajisnik case also charged the accused with persecution, murder, extermination, deportation, and forcible transfer. In assessing whether the remaining crimes fell into category 1 or 3 of the joint criminal enterprise, the Trial Chamber noted: "Whether other crimes were original to the common objective or were added later is, of course, a matter of evidence, not logical analysis." And the Trial Chamber there advocated what it called a "strictly empirical approach" which does not speculate about the crime profile of the original JCE objective but conceptualises the common objective as fluid in its criminal means. Krajisnik trial judgement, paragraph 1098. It explained the means by which the common plan may grow, stating: "An expansion of the criminal means of the objective is proven when leading members of the JCE are informed of new types of crime committed pursuant to the implementation of the common objective, take no effective measures to prevent recurrences of such crimes, and persist in the implementation of the common objective of the JCE. When this occurs, the Trial Chamber said, "JCE members are shown to have accepted the expansion of means since implementation of the common objective can no longer be understood to be limited to commission of the original crimes." Krajisnik judgement at paragraph 1098. The Trial Chamber found that with acceptance of the actual commission of new types of crime and continued contribution to the objective comes intent, and such that subsequent commission of such crimes by the JCE will give rise to liability under JCE 1. Applying this standard, the Krajisnik Trial Chamber found that unlawful detention of civilians, cruel or inhumane treatment of detainees, killings in detention, sexual violence, inhumane living conditions, murder of civilians during attacks on towns and villages, extermination of Muslims, plunder and appropriation of property, destruction of cultural monuments and sacred sites became part of the common objective of the JCE over time, because the Bosnian Serb political leadership was aware of these crimes and did not discontinue its discriminatory forced displacement programme in light of the increasing number and range of crimes being reported but, rather, persisted with its territorial conquest and demographic recompositions. There is extensive similar language, Mr. President, Your Honours, from other cases, but already in the interests of time I will not go into those. The Krstic trial judgement discusses these matters at length, the Kovocka trial judgement discusses similar matters and most recently in the Milutinovic 98 bis decision in May 2007 these matters were discussed. I will pause on the Milutinovic decision to add this additional element in terms of JCE 3. In that case, in a Rule 98 bis submission or determination, the Chamber said this: "In light of the evidence discussed herein pertaining to the significance and organised movement of the Kosovo Albanian population and the behaviour of the accused in relation to these events the Chamber could find that a joint criminal enterprise existed at the relevant time, the aim of which was to forcibly displace the Kosovo Albanian population from Kosovo. Moreover, in the event that some of the specific crimes charged such as rape and murder were not within the common plan, it was nevertheless foreseeable that such crimes might be perpetrated in the course of the mass expulsion of the population." With that little bit of jurisprudence in mind, Your Honours, I'm going to turn to the overview of the Prosecution case. It is the Prosecution case that the crimes that were committed in this case, the crimes charged in the indictment, were part of a top-down leadership-driven geopolitical programme policy and strategy of what can fairly be called the Tudjman-Susak-Boban-Prlic government, because in reality that was seamless. That organisation, the application of power between Tudjman, Susak, Boban, Prlic and others was in fact a seamless operation from Zagreb to Mostar. The events alleged in the indictment occurred as part of the dissolution of course of the former Yugoslavia. The Chamber is quite aware of those background facts. The European Community recognised the Republic of Croatia as an independent state on the 15th of January, 1992, and the United Nations admitted Croatia as a member state on the 22nd of May, 1992. During and in the course of these events, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna declared its existence on the 18th of November, 1991, as a political and territorial entity on the territory of what was then the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As the Chamber knows now, in August 1993, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna declared itself the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Mate Boban was the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna from its inception and continued as president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna until late 1993 and thereafter. By various actions taken on the 8th of April, 1992 and the 15th of May, 1992, various Herceg-Bosna leaders, including Mate Boban, established the Croatian Defence Council or HVO as Herceg-Bosna's armed forces and government describing the HVO as Herceg-Bosna's supreme executive, administrative and defence body. Now, the joint criminal enterprise is stated in the amended indictment in paragraph 15 as follows: "That from on or before 18th of November, 1991," the date that Herceg-Bosna declared its existence, "to about April 1994 and thereafter, various persons established and participated in a joint criminal enterprise to politically and militarily subjugate, permanently remove and ethnically cleanse Bosnian Muslims and other non-Croats who lived in areas on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were claimed to be part of the Croatian Community and later Republic of Herceg-Bosna; and to join these areas as part of a 'Greater Croatia' whether in the short term or over time and whether as part of the Republic of Croatia or in close association with it by force, fear or threat of force, persecution, imprisonment and detention, forcible transfer and deportation, appropriation and destruction of property, and other means which constituted or involved the commission of crimes which are punishable under Articles 2, 3, and 5 of the Tribunal Statute. The territorial ambition of the joint criminal enterprise was to establish a Croatian territory with the borders of the Croatian Banovina, a territorial entity that existed from 1939 to 1941. It was part of the joint criminal enterprise to engineer the political and ethnic map of these areas so that they would be Croat dominated both politically and demographically." Now, turning to the territorial aspects of the joint criminal enterprise. Croatia's President Franjo Tudjman had long given voice to his obsession with Croatia's acquisition of certain parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As included in Dr. Robert Donia's evidence, his report Exhibit P 09536, as early as 1981 Tudjman in his own published work described Bosnia and Croatia as "an indivisible geographic and economic entity." He publicly supported Croatia's claims to large parts of Bosnia which had been part of the Croatian Banovina. As the Chamber knows, the Hrvatska Banovina was a Croat autonomous region established in about 1939 which continued until approximately 1941. It satisfied most of the demands of the two largest national actors in Yugoslavia, the Serbs and the Croats, at the expense of the Bosnian Muslims, with the addition of sovereign BiH territory to the claimed Croatian lands. What I think the evidence shows and what this Tribunal has seen both in this case and in the cases what we might call the Serb cases, with the dissolution of Yugoslavia both Serbia and Croatia saw opportunities for territorial expansion into Bosnia and Herzegovina. Discussions aimed toward the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina were held between Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic at Karadjordjevo in March 1991. On the eve of Croatia breaking free of Yugoslavia, Tudjman made his ambitions toward Bosnian territory vividly clear at a meeting of the Supreme State Council of Croatia on the 8th of June, 1991, which comes from Exhibit P 00037: "Also, gentlemen, if we opt for Croatia's independence either within an alliance or total independence, Croatia's borders such as they are today are absurd. They are impossible in the sense of administration and trade, let alone as regards any kind of protection of these borders of Croatia. Therefore, from our point of view, no less than from the Serbian, there is the problem of, there is a need to find an essential solution to the problem. Isn't that so? Because the establishment of Bosnia, the borders of BiH after World War II are historically absurd."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Scott please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to do that. That is further confirmed in the important meeting which the Chamber's heard a fair amount about, including from the witness Kljuic, who was a participant in the meeting, the important meeting in Zagreb on the 27th of December, 1991, which is recorded in Exhibit P 00089. During that meeting, Tudjman again said: "The survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state, even if possible, is in any case against the interest of the Croatian state and makes impossible the normal territorial establishment of the Croatian state and creates conditions for the disappearance of what remains of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina today. All of history has shown that Bosnia and Herzegovina is no solution for the Croatian people. Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be taken as something God-given, which must be preserved, and we must especially not forget how harmful it is. Because of the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia has been put in an impossible situation regarding its territory. Therefore we finally wanted, and it was no accident that in the preamble to the Croatian constitution we also mentioned the Banovina of Croatia. It seems to me, therefore, that just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent, internationally recognised Croatia, I believe that it is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders." What the Prosecution evidence shows beyond this is that and what really led in a large measure to the conflict was it led President Tudjman and others and the accused in this case to even make claims on territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was not even -- not let alone majority Croat but in many instances not even -- did not even have a plurality of Croat population. This is illustrated by another one of the statements, statement by Tudjman, when he told a group of the Herceg-Bosna representatives meeting with him in September 1993: "Stolac. I know the strategic importance of Stolac both as the president of Croatia and, if you will, as a soldier. I know that Stolac and the entire former Jablanicki Kotar and Konjic were included in the Croatian Banovina in 1939. These are arguments I have upheld since the first day. However, they say that Stolac was predominantly Muslim and therefore ethnic cleansing has taken place." On the 8th of June, 1991, Tudjman indicated that in reality the Muslim leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina would have to accept Bosnia and Herzegovina's division. Tudjman: "I think we shall achieve it because this is equally in the interest of Serbia and Croatia, while the Muslim component has no other exit than to accept this solution, although it will not be easy to find the solution but essentially that is it." Even by October 1993, much later, the quote that I just gave you was Tudjman in June 1991, even by October 1993, Tudjman was still talking about to fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a fight over the borders of the Croatian state. In Exhibit P 06012, Tudjman says: "Several months ago, I told you about the situation, and I gave task to minister of defence Mr. Susak and General Bobetko regarding our help and our engagement -- our engagement in Herceg-Bosna. I told them that this was where the future borders of the Croatian state are being resolved. That is when I pointed out that it was very important that they defended the positions and the territory the HVO was holding there. It was the Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Mostar line and the problems of Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno needed to be solved as soon as possible." Tudjman speaking, October 1993. Now, the Chamber's assisted in this because the question of Croatia's and Tudjman's territorial aspirations have been well established by adjudicated facts which this Chamber has found and I'll refer to some of them here. "President Tudjman aspired to partitioning this neighbouring country, Bosnia-Herzegovina," adjudicated fact number 73 by the Chamber's decision on the 7th of September, 2006. "Franjo Tudjman's nationalism and his desire to annex a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina were apparent to Lord David Owen to whom President Tudjman staked his claim that 17.5 per cent of Bosnian territory should revert to a republic with a Croatian majority." Adjudicated fact number 75. "President Tudjman as the leader of the HDZ, sought to promote a Croatian identity by appealing to Croatia as a distinct and historically continuous entity." Adjudicated fact number 77. Multiple reference to the "natural borders of Croatia" can be found in Tudjman's speeches. Adjudicated fact number 79. "The view that President Tudjman harboured territorial ambitions in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina despite his official position to the contrary, part of his two-track policy, he harboured these ambitions despite his official position to the contrary is strengthened by reports of discussions held between Tudjman and Milosevic against the backdrop of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, Yugoslav Federation, in 1991." Adjudicated fact 81. These aspirations for a partition were furthermore displayed during the confidential talks between Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic in Karadjordjevo on 30 March 1991, on the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Adjudicated fact 82. Excuse me, Judge Prandler. Thank you. "Following Karadjordjevo, Franjo Tudjman opined that it would be very difficult for Bosnia to survive and that the Croats were going to take over the Banovina plus Kazim, Kladusa and Bihac." Adjudicated fact number 84. "Franjo Tudjman also said there would no longer be a Muslim region within the former Yugoslavia, that it would constitute only a small element of the Croat state." Adjudicated fact 89. "The agreement entered into by the Serbs and Croats on the partition of Bosnia was reportedly confirmed by a meeting between the Bosnian Serb and the Bosnian Croat political leaders Radovan Karadzic and Mate Boban in Graz in Austria on 6th May 1992." Adjudicated fact 90. The aspirations of Franjo Tudjman to annex "Croatian regions of Bosnia persisted throughout the conflict." Adjudicated fact number 88, et cetera. And there is more that I won't take the time to read. All of those come from previous ICTY cases, and based upon the Trial Chamber's rulings on adjudicated facts in this case. I will not take the time to look at the maps now, but the Chamber will recall the books of maps that the Prosecution has provided to the Judges in the course of this case, and the Prosecution respectfully submits that one -- all one has to do is look at those maps and map after map after map is consistent with a goal to establish the Banovina borders. It was no coincidence that the outlines, the borders, of Herceg-Bosna were largely co-extensive almost exactly, in fact even a bit more territory, were almost co-extensive with the Banovina borders. Every peace map whether it was Cutileiro, Vance-Owen, every map ever proposed by the Croat side was consistent with establishing the Banovina borders. Now, what have some of our accused said about this aspect of the case? The plan, the Banovina borders, what the joint criminal enterprise was all about. Let's take some of our accused one by one. Mr. Prlic in his statement, Exhibit P 09078, said: "The plan proclaimed and supported by Zagreb, which was also the political centre of power, was, first, to establish the Republic of Croatia's internationally recognised borders. The secondary political goal was to integrate a part of BiH into the Republic of Croatia. Connected to that is the relationship between the HV and the HVO and between the government of the Republic of Croatia and the authorities of Herceg-Bosna. The HDZ in Croatia and BiH were also using the opportunity to address the public and say to the public that everything was being done and all the preparations were being done to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was only partly correct." I'm quoting, quoting from Prlic's statement. Partly true. They said to the public all of these preparations were for the defence exclusively. However, between themselves, they created another plan which was adopted and proclaimed and supported by Zagreb, which was also again the political centre of power. So the goal and the main point of that plan was to defend the territory and possibly also "attach it" to the Republic of Croatia. I have to clearly state that this idea was supported by the majority and most of the people in Herzegovina so was not just a conspiratory plan of one group. Another statement by Mr. Prlic: "Zagreb wanted to integrate a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina into the Republic of Croatia if Bosnia-Herzegovina falls apart." And again at transcript -- the transcript of his statement, page 65: "Most Croats in Herzegovina supported the plan to attach Herceg-Bosna to Croatia." What about -- how did Mr. Slobodan Praljak characterise the plan? Well, actually, it was one of his own exhibits, Exhibit 3D 00482, which was a note of a meeting of Croatian army General Anton Tus and Slobodan Praljak with a French delegation on 13 January 1993. The record of the meeting introduced by the Defence describes Slobodan Praljak as: "Major General Slobodan Praljak, assistant of minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia." Mr. Praljak's statements from the meeting are reported in relevant part as follows: "The Croatian position has been clear from the very beginning. The territory that belongs to the Croats matches the borders of the Banovina Hrvatska from the 1939 division of Yugoslavia synchronised with the 1981 census (the 1991 census is not valid). The Croats stand for Bosnia-Herzegovina as integrity, a state, as well as for the rights of Croats as constitutive nation. The problems among Croats and Muslims are results of a variety of goals within the political fights. The Croats fight for the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the autonomy for Croats while the Muslims fight for the civil state." Now, granted in part of that statement it refers -- Mr. Praljak talks about fighting for the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but he also talks about establishing the Banovina borders, and other statements and other evidence, of course, broaden that statement. What did Mr. Stojic say about the goals of the Bosnian Croats, Tudjman, Boban, and others? Exhibit P 00185 is a recording of a telephone conversation on the 5th of May, 1992, between two Bosnian Croat leaders, Bruno Stojic and Branko Kvesic, and two Bosnian Serb leaders, Bosnian Serb minister of interior Momcilo Mandic, and actually another defendant before this Tribunal, Mr. Mico Stanisic, concerning the Croat's and Serb's territorial claims in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the need for the Croats and the Serbs to sit down and agree their claims together. Of additional interest, it turns out, the conversation occurred only one day before the Graz Agreement on the 6th of May, 1992, which is Exhibit P 00187.

utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the conversation, Stojic plainly indicates that the Croat desired borders are those of the Banovina of 1939. Now, the conversation goes on for some time, and I won't take time to read all of it although reading all of it is quite interesting and makes all of it have more sense, but in the interest of time Stojic and Mico Stanisic are talking, and Stanisic says: "Listen. Karadzic too wants a deal, to sit down and work out a deal, but once it gets started it keeps going." "Bruno: Stop it already what's wrong with you." "Stanisic: Well, let us you give some initiative to have somewhere --" "Bruno: Both you and us. This makes no sense." "Stanisic: We'll give you over here we'll give you Visoko, Vares, Kakanj, and Zenica. We'll give that to you." "Bruno: You can't give us what's ours. You can't give us what's already ours. That is the Banovina of 1939. So what's going on up there? Continuing on in the conversation a couple of minutes later they're talking about the Neretva and Stojic says to Stanisic: "Give up those pipe dreams. What Neretva? You hold on to the Drina." Stanisic says: "There's not a soul for 50 kilometres on either side of the Neretva. I swear to God. Do you agree with me?" "Bruno: But this makes no sense with aeroplanes." "Stanisic: Let's get it started. You give up some, we give up some so we can mark those natural borders and that's it." "Bruno: What natural ones?" "Stanisic: Well, these." "Bruno: There is the 1939 one and none other. I'm dead serious." "Stanisic: We need to see what is realistic there and sit down and make a deal." "Bruno: Only the 1939 borders and no bargaining. Ha, ha." "Stanisic: Don't screw with me. In '39 you didn't even have a state. Ha, ha." How about the accused Mr. Petkovic. In an interesting report on the 26th of June, 1992, which is Exhibit P 00279, just a few weeks after this telephone conversation with Mr. Stojic, Milivoj Petkovic addressed HVO commanders and municipal leaders on the recent HVO military successes in Herceg-Bosna and the remaining work to be done in order to achieve his stated goals, and this is what Mr. Petkovic wrote in his 26 June 1992 document: "1. Operative and tactical situation. Through offensive activities in the entire area of South-east Herzegovina, HVO forces with assistance of considerable HV forces and equipment have achieved success that astonished us all and legal authorities were even taken by surprise. Today we have under control almost the entire area of Croatian municipalities, Neum, Ravno, Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, and Mostar. Admittedly, there is still part of the territory, mostly in Mostar and Stolac municipalities, that are not under control of HVO forces. Therefore, we have four main tasks in front of us." "One, to put under control the remaining area of Croatian -- Croatian municipalities. Two, to secure and fortify the achieved line. Three, to carry out reorganisation of the existing HVO forces and, four, to establish Croatian rule over all municipalities." That was the programme in June 1992. It is the Prosecution case that the HDZ BiH, the party, Herceg-Bosna, and the HVO, instruments used by Tudjman, the Tudjman government, and the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership, including these accused, to pursue a Greater Croatia based largely on the Banovina borders by securing certain BiH municipalities either within Croatia's own borders or in a Croat mini-state which would be closely aligned or identified with Croatia. The problem became, Your Honours, that once it became clear that the Muslims were not going to go down that road voluntarily, it required an escalating series of steps of escalating violence, escalating strategies to do what it took, whatever it took, to achieve the political programme, the geopolitical programme, that I have described to you based on the evidence in the last few minutes. Just as the ICTY Chambers have found the existence of Tudjman's and the Tudjman government's aspirations toward Croatia, there have been extensive adjudicated facts on the control of Croatia over the HVO and Herceg-Bosna establishing the element of an international armed conflict and Croatia's control of the Croat entity. I'm going to again cut through some of the material that I had prepared because I think, really, I can take you straight again to some of the adjudicated facts that this Chamber has already found. "Aside from the direct intervention by HV forces, Croatia exercised indirect control over the HVO and the HZ HB." Adjudicated fact 504. "There is no doubt that the Republic of Croatia enjoyed a strong connection with the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Adjudicated fact 461. "There is no doubt that the Republic of Croatia and the HZ HB were pursuing the same ultimate goals, namely the incorporation of Croatian provinces of Bosnia-Herzegovina into a single Croatian state." Adjudicated fact number 91. "Ties between President Tudjman as head of the HDZ in Croatia and the leadership of the HZ HB were strong throughout the conflict." Adjudicated fact 94. "For Mate Boban, the HDZ was the Bosnian branch of the party founded by Franjo Tudjman." Adjudicated fact 45. "Delegations from the Bosnian HDZ regularly went to consult President Tudjman." Adjudicated fact 98. "There were regular meetings with President Tudjman and the Bosnian Croat leaders appointed by Croatia or with its consent continued to direct - excuse me- and the Bosnian Croat leaders appointed by Croatia or with its consent continued to direct the HZ HB and the HVO well after June 1992." Adjudicated fact 99. "Croatia was thus directly involved in the control of the HVO forces which were created on 8 April by the HZ HB Presidency." Adjudicated fact 471. "The Republic of Croatia took part in the organisation, planning, or coordination of military operations conducted in the context of the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH." Adjudicated fact 474. Your Honours, it's the Prosecution's position that that degree of control itself, without even getting into the specific instances of direct HV Croatian army participation on the ground, even if we don't get to that evidence, the extent of Croatia's utter control of Herceg-Bosna, the Herceg-Bosna leadership and the HVO establishes the existence of an international armed conflict, and the Prosecution does not anticipate directly addressing the more direct military aspects for purposes of this 98 bis submission unless the Chamber has questions, but the evidence of that participation is itself also extensive, down to the exhibits which identify the particular Croatian brigades and units operating on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Going back to the chronology of the -- some of the chronology of the events in relation to Herceg-Bosna, we go back to the 12th of November, 1991, even before it was -- about six days, in fact, before it was declared on the 18th, and there was a meeting of the two major HDZ Regional Committees, one the Herzegovina branch, if you will, led by Mate Boban, and the Central Bosnia community led by Dario Kordic, met in Grude and concluded at that meeting, and the records of that meeting are Exhibit P 00071: "The Herzegovina regional community and the Travnik regional community stand by their conclusions reached at earlier separate meetings that the Croatian people of these regions continue to uphold the unanimously accepted decisions and conclusions adopted during consultations with the president Dr. Franjo Tudjman on 13 and 20 June 1991 in Zagreb. Proceeding from the conclusions of the above-mentioned meetings and consultations in Zagreb and the special conclusion of 15 October 1991 in Grude and 22 October 1991 in Busovaca and this one on 12 November 1991, these two regional communities have jointly and unanimously decided that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally carry out a decisive, a decisive and active policy which should lead to the realisation of our centuries' old dream, a joint Croatian state." In order for this -- continuing in the record: "In order for this historical goal to soon become our reality, these two regional communities request the commencement of activities to formulate and issue legal and political documents (the proclamation of a Croatian Banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina) and a referendum on accession to the Republic of Croatia, et cetera, as the first stage on the road to the final settlement of the issue and the creation of a sovereign Croatia in its ethnic and historical (now possible) borders." Mr. President and Your Honours, the evidence of these matters go on and on and on, and already it's clear that it would take more than the time all of us probably want to take to go through it all, but over and over again, especially in the presidential transcripts, which the Chamber has, which have been admitted, you will see these discussions over and over and over again. Exhibit P 000699, the meeting on the 3rd of November, 1992, often involving a number of our accused, this one including Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, and Bruno Stojic. Again talking about in order to -- Susak was at that meeting. This one I have to mention because some of our accused were there and Susak says: "Furthermore, in order to ensure a better understanding of general policy in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, we called a meeting of the wider region of June -- 20 June 1992, including municipalities. And they got some instructions then. And on the 19th of August, 1992, the following persons were called and present at the meeting in the ministry of defence, Mate Boban, Neven Tomic, Jozo Maric, Bruno Stojic, president --" and this is quoting, "president of the defence department of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Jadranko Prlic, president of the HVO of the HZ HB." And Susak is complaining here: "So it's not true as stated in this report that they didn't know what was Croatian policy regarding Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and what were the guidelines."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, they go on. Exhibit P 01622, 8th of March, 1993. P 02099, 26th April 1993. P 02122, 27th of April, 1993. Exhibit P 03112, 2nd of July, 1993. Exhibit P 05498, the 30th of September, 1993. Exhibit P 06581, 10th of November, 1993. All go on discussing in an ongoing way accomplishing the programme, accomplishing the plan. And the Chamber will, if we don't do it today, and I could stand here and read these to you of course for hours, but I submit that the Chamber -- I invite the Chamber at its leisure to review the presidential transcript material at length, because it is indeed a treasure trove of evidence in this case. Let me just jump to one much later just with the benefit of looking backwards. By February 13th of 1994, still within the period of the indictment, in Exhibit P 07856, Jadranko Prlic is in a meeting with Tudjman and reports to Tudjman the following: "We have created a state in Herceg-Bosna with all systems including customs and finance. People are born and die with Herceg-Bosna documents. I think we should weigh all the elements carefully. Absolutely no solution is acceptable without a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. In other words, a Croatian republic, and the borders should encompass as many areas as possible in the whole of Central Bosnia. I believe we can achieve this by military means if necessary in order to make sure that things are developing the way they are developing." One final exhibit on this point and I'll move forward. Exhibit P 08288, 31 May 1994. This is after the Washington Agreement, but this reveals, Your Honours, that the plan was not dead, the vision was alive, and it was going forward. 31st of May, 1994. Tudjman tells the assembled Herceg-Bosna leaders, including Jadranko Prlic, Dario Kordic, and others: "We must pursue our policy in such a way as to take control of Bosnia without --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you're quoting something, does it appear on the screen, does the evidence or does that particular document appear on the screen so that we can see it very quickly? Did you ask the clerk to do that for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we have not -- again in the interests of time if I was really doing the full show, I would have all that organised for you. We have not had time to do that, but perhaps sometime in the future we can. The Chamber will have to of course check when I give you the exhibit number, and certainly correct, verify my statements, but if I say something is a quote, Your Honour, it's not my word, it's being taken out of the exhibit. I do anticipate hopefully some day perhaps in the closing arguments to be able to perhaps make a fuller presentation on these points. But Tudjman says: "We must pursue our policy, and we will conduct a smart policy. We have to be seen, we have to be seen as siding with the Muslims, but we don't want them to create their Muslim state and that poses a problem." And Tudjman assured the Herceg-Bosna leaders to get the Muslims to declare themselves "Croats of Muslim faith." "Get down to it right now. We have no other choice." Your Honour, then as you -- on that basis the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, the establishment of the HVO itself in April of -- in April and May of 1992. The Chamber will also recall the testimony of witnesses such again as Stjepan Kljuic, Milivoj Gagro. They talked about the political developments in 1991 and to the end of that year, again leading up to the important meeting in Zagreb on the 27th of December, 1991, a meeting which Kljuic attended and gave us his own personal account of and how that was essentially the final big showdown between the moderate arm, if you will, of the HDZ party in Bosnia and the more extremist arm led by Mate Boban, Dario Kordic, and others. And at the end of that meeting it's clear that the moderate arm has lost the day and the extremist and the hard-line arm has won the day, and Tudjman endorses that and again makes a number of final pronouncements in that meeting. In fact, at the conclusion of that meeting again, Exhibit P 00089, Tudjman after hearing all the sides voicing their positions, Tudjman says: "Why not accept offer of demarcation when it is in the interest of the Croatian people, because I do not see a single reason, a serious reason against it. In the event of demarcation, Croatia would not only get those two communities, Herceg-Bosna and the Posavina, but also for geopolitical reasons Cazinska and Bihacka Krajina which would satisfy almost ideally the Croatian national interest and to create a statelet, therefore out of the remaining part around Sarajevo where mostly Muslims and some Catholic Croats would stay which would resemble the small historical land of Bosnia. It would, therefore, be a buffer zone in the demarcation of Serbia and Croatia and in such conditions it would have to rely on Croatia to a large extent. From that viewpoint not even some sort of cannonisation with the continuing existence of Bosnia and Herzegovina would mean for us the solution, which is the solution of demarcation." We then have, Your Honour, a series of exhibits and a series of evidence which talks about and establishes what the Prosecution calls in the indictment and you have heard discussed in the case as the two-track -- two-track policy or approach and that was essentially this: That on the one hand some of the meetings and some of the transcripts that we've already referred to have mentioned this, that there was a very deliberate policy announced by Tudjman, confirmed by others, again if we had the time we could go through transcript after transcript, where basically the policy is this: On the one hand we'll be publicly saying that we support a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, we'll say that we support an undivided Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in reality we have another agenda. In reality, that's the agenda we will be pursuing. At the famous 27 December 1991 meeting there is one example of this. Perica Juric says: "At the diplomatic level our people in Sarajevo can continue swearing they are in favour of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina as we have done so far -- as they have done so far." And Tudjman himself articulated this policy in a meeting with Bosnian Croat leaders in March 1993. This is in Exhibit P 01594. Although the diplomatic climate required that they pay lip-service to a "sovereign BiH" Tudjman made it clear that this was not a permanent situation. "So for the time being, the West is opting for an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina but with a political system that will probably lead to a final solution and few in the world believe that it is possible. If Yugoslavia could not survive, how could Bosnia and Herzegovina survive?" Even months -- that was in December 1991, and even by July 1993, July 1993, in the middle of the core period of this case, in Exhibit P 03195, Tudjman's saying to his assembled leaders, his -- the inside group: "We will not be saying even now that we are openly in favour of dividing Bosnia, just as we recommended in -- to the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina to vote in the referendum when the Serbs had already broken away." But there follows then, Your Honours, and I'm going to summarise very quickly some pages and pages of exhibits and testimony, but by the spring of 1992, the HVO has been established and the Chamber will recall the evidence from various municipal leaders who have told the Chamber about how in municipality after municipality there was the HVO taking power, seizing power, excluding the Muslims from the governments, from businesses. Oh, perhaps there would be a few Muslims that would be left, a few. And how there was the policy of Croatisation. There's got to be Croat curriculum in the schools. The Croatian language has to be used. Croatian currency has to be used. Change the name of street signs to Croatian names. No longer refer to Prozor as Prozor but call it Rama, et cetera, et cetera. And this process goes on throughout 1992, and there's a number of exhibits on that and documents and testimony of the witnesses who talk about that. And again here, and I'm selecting only a few things, but going again to the adjudicated facts, facts that the Chamber can take as a foundation point. "Croat nationalism and discrimination against Muslims was on the increase in Central Bosnia in 1992, 1993." Adjudicated fact 104. "Mostar was politically dominated by the BH Croats." Adjudicated fact 223. "A provision adopted by the Republic of Croatia gave to all members of the Croatian nation the right to citizenship." Adjudicated fact 106. "Another law authorised all Croats to vote in the elections in Croatia thus allowing the Bosnian Croats with Bosnian nationality to vote in the parliamentary elections in the Republic of Croatia." Adjudicated fact 107. "BH Croats could with ease could obtain Croatian passports, enjoy Croatian nationality and vote in elections in the Republic of Croatia." Adjudicated fact 108. "There was a split between Croats and Muslims in 1992." Adjudicated fact 41. Again we saw various aspects of this process in 1992 at work, including taking control of the media. I guess we all know by the first part of the 21st century that one of the first things one tries to do in a situation like this is get control of the media. That was done. The HVO took over the radio station, changed its name to Croat Radio Mostar, et cetera, et cetera. Again by 1994, Jadranko Prlic could report to Tudjman in Exhibit P 04759. "Mr. President, every Croat in Bosnia-Herzegovina is a paid Croat. Everyone is on the salary of the Herceg-Bosna budget except for the part that is in Serbian territory." There has been discussion in the case and various evidence -- various evidence concerning the question of the element of Serb and Croat cooperation in the areas and at the times most relevant to the indictment in this case. I'm going to cut through most of what I had prepared to give you one, I think, example of that that tells the story, if only one piece of evidence could be considered, and that is again a meeting involving Mr. Tudjman and Slobodan Praljak and others, which is Exhibit P 05096, in late September 1993. The scope and nature of the Croat-Serb cooperation and the extent to which it had actually become a critical part of the HVO military process can be seen in that conversation when under international pressure the possibility of peace with the Bosnian Muslims was being considered by Tudjman and his senior advisors, including Praljak, serious concerns were expressed and addressed in that meeting as to how a changed relationship with the Muslims would affect the Croats' good cooperation with the Serbs. "Praljak: The relations between the Croats and the Serbs have improved, especially on the military plane, because our whole units depend on cooperation with the Serbs. In BH this agreement with the Muslims will aggravate that a lot therefore Zepce, Kiseljak and thus Vitez the battalion below Konjic and Vares, it will now be difficult for us to provide them with supplies." And then Tudjman intercedes and says: "Well that may be the case, Praljak, but we've got to do a deal with the Muslims here." Praljak argues that it's going to take time to adjust to this new situation. "Praljak: It will stop," that the fighting with the Muslims will stop, "but this is going to be different. A year ago, we thought we could not hold talks with the Serbs at all, but we have received some agreement with the Serbs --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott is kindly asked to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. "And now we should start a war against them in order to ease the tension with the Muslims, and it will probably take time to turn things around psychologically." "We have to change our thinking. We've been cooperating with the Serbs and now we have to completely change our way of doing things. Some of our units depend on their relationships with the Serbs in Vares, in Kiseljak and other areas." That's what Slobodan Praljak said about cooperation with the Serbs. I then want to address, Your Honours, an element -- a broader element as we go forward in this overview, and as we turn to the fall of 1992, what is the environment, what is the context in which these things have all been happening? The war in the former Yugoslavia has now already been going on for some time, and the Prosecution believes that it is important for the Chamber to note that these armed conflicts, persecutions, ethnic cleansings, and mass detentions in the former Yugoslavia didn't just begin in 1993 with this indictment. By August 1992, as reflected in Exhibit P 05096; the UN Security Council had already repeatedly expressed its "grave alarm at the widespread violations of international humanitarian law in the former Yugoslavia," including "mass forcible expulsion and deportation of civilians, imprisonment and abuse of civilians in detention centres, deliberate attacks on non-combatants, impeding the delivery of food and medical supplies to the civilian population, and wanton -- excuse me -- devastation and destruction of property." It -- the Security Council "strongly condemned" any violations of international humanitarian law including those involved in the practice of what was already by August 1992 being called "ethnic cleansing." Much of this information in this particular aspect I will summarise it this way, Your Honours, and there is a lot of this evidence in the record, there's extensive documentation of the UN, Resolution after Resolution, report after report establishing what even by mid-1992 had already occurred and already characterised the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. The Chamber may recall that Dr. Miller summarised much of this evidence in his report, Exhibit P 10239, titled "The Characteristics and Patterns of the Balkan Conflict as Widely-Known and Reported by the Latter Part of 1992." Dr. Miller concluded in his report, which I think aptly summarises substantial body of evidence on this, but we don't have time to go through it all this afternoon: "Throughout 1991 and by the summer and autumn of 1992, the dominant characteristics of a conflict based on ethnicity and the practices and patterns of behaviour involved in such conflict became and were widely reported, publicly recognised, and well-understood. Attacks on civilians, forcible population transfers, and large-scale detentions were already a known part of what was already called 'ethnic cleansing'." Dr. Miller went on to conclude: "Any moderately informed person living and working in the former Yugoslavia could not but have known of these developments and reports and the characteristics and practices involved in the Balkan conflict. The actions of the warring sides through the middle of 1992, illustrate clearly that killings of civilians, forced expulsions and widespread destruction would ensue, would ensue should any ethnic group try to subjugate another in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The ethnic nature of the conflict was clear before it ever began as the violence in Plitvice, Borovo Selo, and Pakrac demonstrate. The likelihood of violence against civilians was made clear by events in Dalj, Tenja, and literally dozens of other individual cases examples of which were examined above" in his report. That is the knowledge environment or the information environment, if you will, that already existed by mid-1992, before any of the significant crimes in had this case had been committed. And in fact that takes us up to October of 1992 and the first major breakout of Muslim and Croat fighting at Prozor and Novi Travnik at the end of October of 1992. In light of what Dr. Miller summarised for us and in fact and as Boban himself predicted, most Bosnian Muslims did not, would not, accept HVO control even when it was thrust upon them. By the latter part of 1992, it was clear that Tudjman's and the Herceg-Bosna's leadership Greater Croatia project could not be achieve only by political pressure or what might be called the softer forms of persecution. It was clear that more forcible action would be required with ethnic violence, armed conflict, and forcible involuntary transfers. In fact, the Croatian and Herceg-Bosna leadership were already preparing for the conflict even just a few weeks before the outbreak of fighting in Prozor in October. Again, in a meeting on the 11th of September, 1992, Exhibit P 00466, Slobodan Praljak told Tudjman and Susak: "War with the Muslims can be anticipated." And Susak answers Praljak: "We have been aware of that for over a week now, and we have made preparations on what needs to be done." 11 September 1992, Prozor, 23 October 1992. In that same meeting the conversation continues: "Tudjman: Gentlemen, gentlemen. Let's not or generality -- we have nothing to conquer. Let's defend those Croatian --" And Praljak jumps in: "Nowhere, Mr. President. It is impossible to pass further. "Tudjman: And let's get ready." 11th of September, 1992. "Let's get ready to cleanse them out of Croatia. As I said, do not get involved in conquering Bosnia." "Praljak: No, Mr. President, believe me, the attacks have been stopped." "Susak: Nothing out of the Banovina. We did not trespass, not even one metre." "Praljak: Believe me, we would be there within 12 hours, in the empty Nevesinje, Trebinje, without any problem." "Susak: There is no problem for us to enter tomorrow. We can't because that's how it is." "Tudjman: Don't, because -- listen, we have to be -- let's be realistic. We have hardly escaped both the Islamic government and the world to have sanctions imposed on us because we are allegedly also aggressors in Bosnia, those who are conquering Bosnia. Accordingly don't do it." That is, don't go one step beyond the Banovina. Susak responds: "President, we are disciplined to the maximum." In a second meeting a few days later involving many of the same participants, on the 26th of September, 1992, so again only a short time prior to Prozor, on the 26th of September, 1992, in Exhibit P 00524, Slobodan Praljak warns Tudjman and Susak of the danger presented by the influx of Muslim refugees in the parts of Herceg-Bosna, in parts of Herzegovina claimed by Herceg-Bosna. And Praljak gives his advice to Tudjman and Susak: "Better to deal with the situation now during a time of war because it would be difficult to expel them later." Exhibit P 00524 at pages 17 and 18. Praljak talking: "There were some talks in the government that the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina should be allowed to enter Croatia in anyway and at any price since these refugees are already on the territory where the Croatian people are. Then from Croatia under the pressure of the international community they should be sent to the border and to hell with them. As it seems now, and due to the people settling on the territory from Travnik and below, I am afraid our chances will be bad at the moment when the war is over. There's been a great change in the ethnic structure, and to solve that with them by war, the civil, international rights," the conversation is a bit, sporadic but "the civil, international rights et cetera, it will be difficult in any form to expel those people from there and without expelling those people we will not have a majority." Praljak in September 1992. As so often happens the case, I realise we are coming up to the time for the break, but what see also, what the evidence shows again and again, Your Honours, is a -- the delivery of an HVO and HDZ demand or ultimatum rejected by the Muslims and then followed up by action, force by the HVO. And that's exactly what we saw in Prozor in October 1992, what we saw in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, what we see in Central Bosnia and in Sovici Doljani in April 1993, over and over and over again the same pattern repeats itself. On the 23rd of October 1992 in Exhibit P 00628, just days after the conversations between Praljak, Tudjman and Susak we've talked about in the last few minutes, the HVO leadership in Prozor insist that the Muslims accept the HVO political and military structures, and in that document they say this, they make these demands on the Muslims: One, we demand an urgent and unconditional cessation of all military operations. Two, we insist on an urgent dispatch of all your soldiers to bring up to strength the units at the first combat line towards the Chetniks, of course. Three, withdrawal of all armed units from the town. Four, passage for the military police units coming from outside our municipality on their way to their final destination as per their combat task. And five, and most importantly for this purpose, we insist on an urgent and instant acceptance of the civilian and military structure of the HVO HZ HB in which Muslims' representatives will also be -- will also participate proportionally they say. Instant acceptance of the civilian and military structure of the HVO. Well, the Muslims again say no, and then we have the fighting in Prozor on the 23rd and 24th of October, 1992. Now, there couldn't have been much of a fight because by the 24th of October, 1992, in Exhibit P 00647, the HVO operative zone commander Zeljko Siljeg reports up the HVO chain of command: "The town of Prozor and Rama Lake are under the control of the Prozor HVO. These two areas are ethnically pure. The Muslim population has been detained or has fled." As of the 24th of October, 1992. I'm looking at the clock and my outline. That would be a good time to break if that's agreeable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just before we leave Prozor, October of 1992, we of course do not want to leave Mr. Coric out of the picture, and Exhibit P 00956 is Mr. Coric's report on the work of the HVO military police covering really the period from its foundation in April 1992 to the end of the year 1992. The report itself dated the 26th December 1992. And I might just invite the Chamber to -- it's one of those few exhibits that covers the entire period from the formation of the military police to the end of that year. That is a source of a great deal of information should the Chamber wish to peruse it. In that report, Mr. Coric says about Prozor: "On 23 October, 1992, there was an armed clash between members of the BH army and the HVO in Prozor and military police units intervened. Within a short time, the town was under the control of the military police. On the military police side, one member was killed and five were wounded. At the same time, there was a clash in Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno." At the same time, and to put this in a broader context, in that same report Mr. Coric reported on the 21st of October, 1992, regarding a worsening situation in Central Bosnia, a complete blockade of the town of Mostar was achieved. Five hundred military policemen took part in that operation. So the HVO military police were also at work under Mr. Coric's leadership. By the end of 1992, which we've now arrived at, and early 1993, there are - excuse me - the developments of the Vance-Owen peace proposals and discussions. While neither the Serbs or Muslims had agreed to the Vance-Owen proposals by mid-January 1993, and, yes, there were some pieces that some agreed to, sometimes there would be part of the map or some part of the plan. So there's no confusion on that. There were times when certain parts would be accepted but never the entire plan. And while neither the Serbs nor the Muslims had agreed to the plan, by mid-January of 1993, Tudjman, Susak, and the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership, including the accused, found the Vance-Owen proposals as they envisioned and as they interpreted them much to their favour. Once again essentially by the borders of the Vance-Owen provinces 3, 8, and 10, essentially giving them the Banovina borders. The problem being again this despite the fact that many of the areas included within those borders had majority or at least equal Muslim populations but not agreed or consented to be part of Herceg-Bosna. Indeed, the Vance-Owen proposal appeared to give the Croats, who at that time comprised approximately 17.5 per cent of the overall BiH population, approximately 28 per cent of BiH's overall territory. Tudjman himself later stated in June 1993, in Exhibit P 02613, that the proposed Vance-Owen provinces 3, 8, and 10 were in fact "roughly what in 1939 became part of the Banovina of Croatia." It was because of this apparent favourable treatment that the Croats received under the Vance-Owen discussions, again at least as interpreted by them, that the saying began circulating in Zagreb in BiH that HVO stood for "Hvala, Vance-Owen." By mid-January 1993, the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership was so eager, in fact, to implement their vision of the Vance-Owen proposal that they refused to wait for the Muslims and Serbs to accept their interpretation and instead took unilateral action to implement it. At a meeting in Zagreb again on the 15th of January 1993, which is recorded in Exhibit P 01158, Tudjman, Susak, and Boban failed to convince Bosnia-Herzegovina's President Alija Izetbegovic - this is also a meeting attended on the record by Alija Izetbegovic - failed to convince Izetbegovic to accept their views. The 15th of January, 1993. And then immediately set out to implement their plans in any event. Izetbegovic complained during this meeting that the Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities had disenfranchised the Muslims of Mostar, who comprised half the city's population and that the HZ HB and HVO authorities had elsewhere dissolved legal governments. Izetbegovic also drew attention to the fact that Tudjman, Susak, and Boban were interpreting the Vance-Owen Plan as a green light to force the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to withdraw from the three regions of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Croat leaders considered theirs. Izetbegovic makes it very clear in this meeting -- read the transcript, and he makes it very clear on the 15th of January that's not his position, that's not his view. "Izetbegovic: That's not how I understood the papers, and I don't know whether this was the intention of these documents, because I do not see that they define who has what territories, whose armies these are, you know. So I'm afraid what is now going on in Gornji Vakuf may have been caused by a misunderstanding of this item of these agreements." Izetbegovic goes on: "I don't think this was foreseen in any of these proposals. It was not foreseen that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina should leave either the Travnik province or Mostar. That's not how I understood these papers." On the same day, 15th of January, 1993, notwithstanding Izetbegovic's unequivocal position reject being the HVO position, the HVO President Jadranko Prlic signed a decision that "all units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which at this moment are stationed in provinces 3, 8, and 10, which have been declared Croatian provinces in the Geneva Accords, shall be subordinated to the command of the Main Staff of the HVO armed forces. The deadline for implementing this decision is hereby set at five days starting from today, 15 January 1993." And that is Exhibit P 01155. Now, Your Honours, we see in this instance a full demonstration of the HVO chain of command, because first it starts with the decision that I just quoted by Jadranko Prlic, P 01155, and immediately following on that the defence minister or department head Bruno Stojic issues his order, Exhibit P 01140, specifically referencing the Prlic decision, which then is followed in turn, just as you would expect it, president, Ministry of Defence, top military professional or soldier followed by the corresponding order of the chief of the HVO Main Staff Milivoj Petkovic, which is Exhibit P 01139. Issued up and down the chain of command all on the 15th of January, 1993, with Petkovic's order again specifically referring by description and number to the Prlic decision and the Stojic order. Once again, the core of these facts is established, at least in part, by the adjudicated facts. "Mate Boban, the leader of the HDZ BiH immediately agreed to the terms of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan as it promised huge gains in territory for the Bosnian Croats." Adjudicated fact 126. "Mate Boban signed the Vance-Owen Plan on behalf of the BH Croats on 2 January 1993. Neither the BH Serbs nor the BH Muslim representatives had signed the plan at this stage." Adjudicated fact 128. "Despite knowing that the other parties had not signed, but filled with confidence that they had the world's opinion behind them, the BH Croats attempted to implement the Vance-Owen Plan unilaterally." Adjudicated fact 129. Despite the fact that neither the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, nor the international peace negotiators had agreed to the unilateral implementation of their views of the Vance-Owen proposals, the HVO authorities and forces with the passage of the deadline set in the Prlic decision took military and violent actions to enforce the ultimatum, attacking and pressing the Muslims at a number of locations including at Novi Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, as charged in the indictment, and Busovaca. That is, of course, this Tribunal. Izetbegovic again makes it clear, he says, that the Croatian leadership interpreted the provisions of the plan in a completely erroneous manner. By the way that the rule worked, it disproportionately affected by a huge factor, primarily the Muslim refugees and displaced persons that had gathered in Mostar, in the Mostar area around that time, and there was one of the international organisations, I won't mention the name because it was a protected witness, who said that this decision was nothing less than a form of ethnic cleansing by administrative decree. The systematic nature of the step-by-step removal of Muslims from Herceg-Bosna's claimed territory is evidenced also by the imprisonment of much of their intelligentsia. Throughout the spring of 1993 there was a series of arrest and imprisonment of the religious, political and intellectual leadership, even before the events in May, that is the attack on Mostar. In early 1993, the HVO imprisoned in fact roughly 100 Muslim intellectuals. In April, May, and June 1993, any Imams who could be captured by the HVO were arrested, and dozens -- a dozen, excuse me, were taken prisoner at that time. Underscoring that Muslim intellectuals were singled out for special treatment is the fact that they were largely gathered and confined in one particular location, and that was the HVO prison at Ljubuski. And you heard evidence about that, and there's evidence in the record about some of the men who were taken to that location and held for a long, long time. Ethnic cleansing moved forward during the summer of 1993, of course, as all Muslim men of military age were arrested despite international warnings to the Croat authorities that this was against international humanitarian law. It can also be noted in the context of the events in -- from the late spring and summer and fall of 1993 that the HVO actions typically followed a pattern time after time, whether it was in Prozor, Stolac, Capljina, other areas. First, most of the Muslim military-aged men, sometimes described as between 60 -- 16 and 60, they would be rounded up, arrested and detained at various HVO prisons and concentrations leaving the women, the children and the elderly in the villages unprotected by adult men. Then with most of the Muslim men removed, the HVO took control of the towns and villages, systematically rounded up Bosnian Muslim women, children, and elderly and then either deported them or sent them off in other directions to perhaps ABiH controlled territory. There were a number of practices, in fact, all the -- those involved in this joint criminal enterprise followed and used. There was the use of force, intimidation and terror. In the course of the mass arrest and evictions, Bosnian Muslims were killed, severely injured, sexually assaulted, robbed of their property, otherwise abused. Identity papers and similar documents were routinely taken from them placing them at various risk of not having the proper papers, limiting their freedom of movement. There was also a pattern of appropriation and destruction of property. Herceg-Bosna authorities and soldiers forced Bosnian Muslims to abandoned their homes, often to actually sign them over, leave the keys. Money, cars, and personal property were often taken or looted. Muslim dwellings and other buildings including public buildings and services were appropriated, destroyed, severely damaged, together with Muslim religious buildings, schools, and mosques. The Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities appropriated public property belonging to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We see that even in the decrees of the government that you'll find in the Narodni List. We hereby seize and take over appropriate all public property formerly belonging to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is the internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
