And I'm going to leave most of that particular discussion to the considerations of the Coric and Pusic submissions, because in the Prosecution's view and the submissions that we will make, both of those two accused feature very substantially in the deportation, the use of letters of guarantee, transit visas by which the Muslims were systematically moved out of not only Herceg-Bosna but out of the country to other areas. The Chamber also heard extensive evidence about the denial and blockage of humanitarian aid as a means -- essentially as a -- as a weapon of war. We're not going to dwell on that for these particular 98 bis purposes, which would make these submissions even longer but the Prosecution notes and the Chamber will recall extensive evidence by which humanitarian convoys were blocked, looted, humanitarian aid was blocked from entering towns and cities, in particular Mostar, in which there was a siege and in which no humanitarian aid was able to enter the city for approximately a two-month period, until the 25th of August, 1993, when the Chamber heard from various witnesses a final convoy -- or a convoy was finally able to enter into Mostar at the end of August. In terms of the movement of both people and aid, in fact, that is the passage of people and aid through Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Praljak has confirmed to the Trial Chamber that is he, Mr. Praljak, Bruno Stojic, Milivoj Petkovic and others controlled the passage of people and aid. And that's in the trial transcript, page 19331 to 19332. There was the widespread -- there was the widespread practice of forced labour. Again, won't go into the details of that now. I think the Chamber has heard extensive evidence. You have the documentation, you have the journals, you have the documents by which on a daily basis prisoners were taken, for example, from the Heliodrom for labour at the Mostar confrontation line and other places. Highly systematic over a long period of time. Hardly can be explained by the conduct of rogue units, of rogue individuals. Highly systematized record-keeping, journals, books every prisoner who was taken back, every prisoner who came back, some of them who didn't come back or were killed or wounded. Turning to the events around Mostar on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993. Ultimately, Your Honours, I'll just say ultimately it doesn't really matter. We've heard a lot of evidence and a lot of argument about who started it. Now, it is -- the Prosecution submits it's the weight of the evidence and the reports of every single international observer without exception, every single international monitor, observer indicated it was the HVO who initiated this action; but even if it wasn't, it doesn't change anything. Because there's no question what happened on those days in terms of the mass arrests and expulsions of Muslims from West Mostar, either pushed over into East Mostar or taken to the Heliodrom where they were kept at least for -- initially for a period of some days. Many were then released and then many imprisoned again later. So we need not spend too much time on deciding necessarily, although it is the Prosecution position that the HVO initiated it. Who fired the first shot on the 9th of May determines really nothing because we know what happened on that day. The evidence is clear. Women and children were taken to the Vales football stadium. They were rounded up, they were put on buses, and they were taken to the Heliodrom. Soon afterwards we had again, once again, the UN Security Council Resolution strongly condemning what had happened in Mostar. That is Exhibit P 02274. The council demands that the attacks against the areas of Mostar, Jablanica, and Dreznica cease forthwith, that Bosnian Croat paramilitary units withdraw immediately from the area and that all parties strictly comply with their previous commitments as well as the cease-fire agreed to today between the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Bosnian Croat party." The Security Council also expresses its deep concern that the UNPROFOR battalion in the area," we know that to be the Spanish Battalion, "has been forced under fire to redeploy as a result of this latest offensive and condemns the refusal of Bosnian Croat paramilitary units to allow the presence of United Nations military observers, in particular in the city of Mostar." "The Security Council calls upon the Republic of Croatia in accordance with the commitments under the Zagreb agreement of 25 April 1993, to exert all its influence on the Bosnian Croat leadership and paramilitary units with a view to ceasing immediately their attacks, particularly in the areas of Mostar, Jablanica, and Dreznica." "It further calls on the Republic of Croatia to adhere strictly to its obligations under Security Council Resolution 752, including putting an end to all forms of interfering -- interference and respecting the territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." I'll just note here in terms of the -- going back to the topic of international armed conflict in the control and presentation of -- or the control of the Croatian government presence of Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness Galbraith, Peter Galbraith, the former US ambassador said it well when he said that everyone knew that what was happening in Herceg-Bosna was controlled by Zagreb. His lines were and I didn't specifically look it up but it's very close to this: "It was an open secret verging on being no secret at all." That was one of the better lines of testimony in the trial so far. "It was an open secret verging on being no secret at all." If you wanted to have something done in Herceg-Bosnia, if you wanted to have Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic or Slobodan Praljak do something in Herceg-Bosna, you pushed the buttons in Zagreb. And Galbraith testified to that as have other witnesses. And in this case we see it -- and the reason I mention it now is because we see it here in the Security Council Resolution. Why because of the fighting in Mostar does the Security Council call on the Republic of Croatia to stop the fighting? I've been told that the reference to that testimony by Mr. Galbraith is at transcript page 6471, line 5. On the 11th of May, 1993, after the second day of the Croat assault on Mostar, Tudjman met again with senior Croatian government and military officials and once again confirmed his understanding that Izetbegovic's provisional acceptance of the Vance-Owen Plan was not an admission by Izetbegovic that provinces 3, 8, and 10 were to become "Croatian." And that is in Exhibit P 02302. Tudjman admits in that meeting: "When the Muslim leadership accepted the Vance-Owen Plan, they did it only formally. Izetbegovic never accepted that Vance-Owen Plan, because these provinces should have been Croat." Franjo Tudjman. Izetbegovic never accepted the Vance-Owen Plan. On the 20th of May, 1993, in Exhibit P 02466, Tudjman reports that he told Izetbegovic that: "Croats surely cannot agree to lose some areas that used to be part of the Banovina, even though 140.000 of refugees are accommodated in those provinces out of what number of Muslims is a hundred thousand." "Croatia as a country cannot accept the change in the demographic structure of those areas." By June of 1993, the HVO forces had commenced a siege against East Mostar, a veritable siege. Yes, there was a mule trail over the mountains, a very difficult trail, that some people could go and come from Mostar, but certainly not a four-lane highway. There was a siege, there was shelling, there were snipers. There was the deprivation of food, humanitarian aid, medical treatment. There was the shelling and sniping that the Chamber has heard so much about. And I would note in this context another exhibit, Defence Exhibit of Mr. Praljak, 3D 00482. This is a note from a meeting of Croatian army General, again, Anton Tus - it's the same record that we talked about earlier - with a French delegation on the 13th of January, 1993. Also including again Mr. Praljak. Praljak says: "The Serbs have predominance in artillery, which is, however, not decisive. Artillery is used for destruction of towns without military goals. They never hit the first combat lines. The same is going on in Sarajevo, Mostar, Jajce, Bosanski Brod, Slavonski Brod, and elsewhere. Their tactic is to destroy the defence by using dead children, women, and elderly." I leave it to the Chamber to decide whether that same language what Mr. Praljak attributes to the Serbs and the artillery shelling of towns could be applied to the HVO shelling of East Mostar. After an ABiH attack on an HVO camp in the northern part of Mostar on the 30th of June, and there's no doubt about that, the Prosecution has never questioned and will not question, will never question that there was a war going on. There was fighting between combat elements on both sides, and there was indeed an ABiH attack on the northern barracks in Mostar, on the northern part of Mostar on the 30th of June. No question about that. Soldiers on soldiers. Military on military. That results in a statement, a decision and order being issued by Jadranko Prlic and Bruno Stojic on the 30th of June. That is Exhibit P 03038. And in that document, again over the names and signatures of both Prlic and Stojic, there is a proclamation stating that now Croat civilians are being exterminated. The very existence of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina was in extreme and imminent danger, that Mostar was and would remain a Croatian town. And again in -- to put it in the broader context, on the 2nd of July, just two or three days after the 30th of June, of course, excuse me, Franjo Tudjman told Susak and others meeting in Zagreb that it was "important to put pressure on the Muslim units on the Neretva front." Here again we have an absolutely, well, as close to perfect as I suppose we can get, of an instance of the HVO chain of command at work. In January, you will remember, we had the Prlic decision, the Stojic order and the Petkovic order all implementing the January 15th, 1993, ultimatum. Here we have the issuance of the Prlic-Stojic decision and order. Again that's P 03038, followed by a communication, P 03039, a communication by Zeljko Siljeg, commander of the north-west operative zone who is already transmitting the Prlic and Stojic order and it's in the document by number, it's exactly the Prlic-Stojic order, transmitting that down his chain of command in the north-west operative zone in P 03039. On the same day, in P 03019, General Petkovic issues his order, same day, and says: "In units where you still have Muslim soldiers, disarm and isolate them. Isolate all able-bodied men in Muslim inhabited villages in your area of responsibility and leave women and children in their homes or apartments." That's the order of Petkovic following the order and decision by Prlic and Stojic. At the bottom of that Petkovic order is the next order by Miljenko Lasic, the operative zone commander for the south-east operative zone which includes Mostar, and what Lasic has done is he's written on the bottom of the Petkovic order passing it on down his chain of command, forwarding the Petkovic order to the HVO 2nd and 3rd Brigades. Then you have on the same day, the 30th of June, P 03035, the order in fact by the HVO 3rd Brigade, now we're down to the brigade level, implementing the referenced Miljenko Lasic order: "In units which still have fighters of Muslim nationality, disarm and isolate. In places with Muslim population within the area of responsibility isolate all able-bodied men. Women and children are to be left in their houses." Almost quoting the Petkovic order. Next we have in P 03075, the next day, 1 July 1993, again, we don't want to leave the military police out, we have the report from the 3rd Company, 3rd Battalion, HVO military police for the 30th of June and the 1st of July, 1993. "On the 30th of June at 0900 hours, a group of 17 military policemen went on a mission to Mostar on orders of the military police administration. A general mobilisation of the remaining members of the company was carried out. As a result, one platoon was engaged in collecting persons of Muslim faith in Stolac, and the other performed the regular duties of securing facilities and manning the check-points. The platoon in Neum also performed its regular duties and in addition to those collected, collected, the above-mentioned persons. The platoon on stand-by escorted, received, and secured the apprehended persons. So far about 1.300 persons have been apprehended and brought in from the municipalities of Stolac, Capljina, Mostar, and Neum on 30 June and 1 July 1993." Thirteen hundred. "Apprehending and bringing in were carried out in cooperation with the Capljina Ministry of the Interior police brigade and the 1st Knez Domagoj Brigade." Also on the same day, 1 July 1993, we have another -- a second Petkovic order, P 03082. To all HVO operative zones and brigades: "Undertake vigorous measures toward each HVO member who does not carry out his duties extremely conscientiously and responsibly. No arbitrariness, superficiality or irresponsibility in work on anybody's part may be tolerated any more. Six, it must be clear to everybody that only Croats will defend the HZ HB." On the 2nd of July 1993, we have Exhibit P 03128, still another Petkovic order, this time also signed as -- by Bruno Stojic as indicating his agreement to the order to all HVO operative zones and units, again up and down the line "with the aim of eliminating the Muslim armed forces and carrying out a final showdown (mopping up the Muslim armed forces defence forces.) Including the HVO military police and also civilian police and Home Guard Units. You are given all authority over military and civilian organs." And in fact goes on to say: "Until the assigned tasks are completed, you are directly subordinated to the HVO General Staff." Until all these units -- until this is accomplished, you are directly subordinated to the HVO general or Main Staff. On the 6th of July, 1993, we have Exhibit P 03234, an order by Zeljko Siljeg, the commander of the north-west operative zone: "In accordance with the current situation in the area of Rama, Prozor municipality, I hereby order arrest and detain all Muslim men aged between 16 and 60. The following are responsible for carrying out of this order: The military police and the SIS, the Security Information Service, of the Rama Brigade." Those are just six or seven of the orders from the 30th of June, 1st of July, 2nd of July, and the 6th of July, all indicating and initiating the mass arrests, that the Chamber knows from the evidence, the mass arrest of Muslim men and imprisonment of them starting in July 1993, taken to the various camps, whether it be Heliodrom, Ljubuski, Dretelj, Gabela, or otherwise. Top down. Orders from the top down to the brigade and company level. On this question in terms of where we're talking about military orders and the chain of command, there appears to be no question, of course, about the commanders at the top of the HVO military during the spring of 1993 and continuing until November 1993. Prior to Mr. Praljak becoming head of the HVO military in the latter part of July 1993, Mr. Petkovic was the head of the HVO armed forces in terms of being the chief military officer. After Mr. Praljak took the top position, as he has told us himself, and I'm quoting from the trial transcript at page 24 -- 24314: "So the commander of the Main Staff, that was me, and the deputy commander, well, can we set that straight and determine who was who, what was what, the commander and the witness can say whether this was right or not, the commander of the Main Staff was Slobodan Praljak. The deputy commander of the Main Staff was General Milivoj Petkovic. The Chief of Staff, General Tole. The deputy chief of the Main Staff was General Matic." And we should also review in discussing these senior HVO military commanders the expert report and testimony of General Pringle. His expert report is Exhibit P 09549. What were some of General Pringle's key points? First of all, HVO was not started from scratch. There was prior preparation and existing doctrine from the JNA giving both Petkovic and Praljak the tools to command and impose disciplinary standards, including quite extensive training and materials, manuals on the International Law of War, et cetera, which General Pringle covered extensively in his report. Number two, Pringle assessed that: "The HVO documentation enshrined the concept of political control over the military, as one would expect." That's at page 6 and 7 of his report. General Pringle discussed with the Chamber the important concept of command climate, the atmosphere created by a commander and is set by example -- which is set by example and not just rules and regulation. He talked about -- he gave the example of a commander talking about the opposition in "derogatory and dismissive ways, such as using the term 'balija,' as sending a message to the troops and those, your subordinates, about appropriate attitudes and treatment toward them." I'll finish on this point, Your Honour. I think I can finish in two more minutes about General Pringle's testimony. General Pringle did tell us also that the more confused the situation the greater the commander's responsibility. Now, again no one has ever said that there isn't confusion in the war situation. The Prosecution's never said to the contrary. But what General Pringle told us was the more confused the situation, in fact the greater the commander's responsibility. General Pringle of course told us that military discipline is important. The failure to impose discipline will be taken as an acceptance and even approval of such behaviour and such actions that are not disciplined or not punished, such actions will become "commonplace." He even assessed, General Pringle in his testimony, transcript page 24059, Praljak seemed to show he had the character to impose discipline if he wanted to. General Pringle also said a commander must be aware of what troops under his command are doing. The Chamber may remember his two up, two down analysis. You must know what your subordinates are doing and be informed, keep yourself informed. You have an obligation, a duty to keep yourself informed. Commanders must follow up orders to ensure they are carried out. The Chamber heard General Pringle say a number of times, giving the order is the easy part. Making it happen is more difficult. General Pringle also indicated when large numbers of people were detained, the commanders - at that particular time it was Mr. Petkovic in the top position - should have been aware of the logical issues involved -- excuse me, the logistical issues involved, food, water shelter, et cetera. And again, General Pringle's position was also a pragmatic one. He says well, of course, maybe on the first day, maybe on the second day you're going to have a problem. You can't fix everything at once. But what General Pringle said was by day ten, he should have been asking how all these detainees were being accommodated and fed and taken care of. And I'll conclude, Your Honour, with this from General Pringle: He concluded his report, again Exhibit P 09549: "The HVO faced a significant challenge," and he said that. "The HVO faced a significant challenge. Setting up the community of Herceg-Bosna, forming and training an army, and drawing up all the regulations and laws to underpin the HZ HB whilst engaging in an actual conflict, first with the Bosnian Serbs and then with the Bosnian Muslims." All this would have presented enormous difficulties. That said, much of the documentation that I have been presented with by the Office of the Prosecutor indicates --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. That said, much of the documentation that I have been presented with by the Office of the Prosecutor indicates in my opinion a working governmental system with a military answerable to the civilian leadership and with orders and instructions flowing down the chain of command from the Presidency via the department of defence and the Main Staff to the operational commands. A working army subject to laid-down military code of discipline was plainly in existence. It relied heavily on poorly trained, locally raised forces and suffered from a lack of trained regular military manpower. This would have placed considerable demands on the training system and on officer corps, many of whom were not fully trained themselves. That said, there are doctrinal documents, particularly those pertaining to compliance with the international laws of war, that had they been followed would have resulted in reasonable military behaviour. The onus on commanders to set a proper example and insist on proper standards of discipline was great, particularly the ex-regular officers of the JNA who would have received a proper and conventional military training. I'll stop there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Before I continue on, I have to make one correction. I've been told that I referred to an exhibit by number P 01737 today on page 48 of the transcript, line 8, and it should have been Exhibit P 01739. Continuing on, Mr. President, again I come to a part of our submission where the Chamber can be assisted by the adjudicated facts that it has found in connection with not only Mostar but what was happening in Herzegovina during this time, the summer of 1993. "There was a widespread and systematic attack against the Muslim part of the civilian population in the area relevant to the indictment. This campaign had a specific aim to transform the formerly ethnically mixed area in and around Mostar into BH Croat territory to be populated by an ethnically pure BH Croat population." That is adjudicated fact 156. "Thousands of Muslim civilians were forced to leave their homes in Sovici, Doljani, and West Mostar." That is adjudicated fact 157. "The campaign against the BH Muslim population in the area reached a climax after the attack on Mostar in early May, 1993, when following the hostilities, the BH Muslim given population was forced out of West Mostar in concerted actions." Adjudicated fact 158. "The harassment of BH Muslims by forcing them out of their apartments and detaining them became common and widespread from 9 May throughout the autumn of 1993." Adjudicated fact 159. "BH Muslim religious sites like the mosques in Sovici and Doljani were systematically destroyed." Adjudicated fact 160. "Detention facilities for the BH Muslim part of the population were established all over the area." Adjudicated fact 162. "Prisoners were moved around between places and detention centres. For example, the ABiH soldiers who surrendered or were captured in Sovici and Doljani were brought to the Ljubuski prison on 18 April 1993, and were later moved to the Heliodrom." Adjudicated fact 163. "Detained BH Muslim civilians and BH Muslim soldiers out of combat were often subjected to humiliating and brutal mistreatment by soldiers who had unfettered access to the detection facilities." Adjudicated fact 164. "Many Muslim civilians and prisoners of war were beaten and otherwise severely mistreated in various detention facilities and the soldiers who engaged in this came from various military units." Adjudicated fact 165. Now, continuing on, in the summer of 1993 we have further indications or evidence of the accused Bruno Stojic in connection with the course of the events especially concerning the Muslim population in Mostar which was confirmed at a dinner meeting with international observers in mid-July 1993, which the Chamber just heard about again recently in some of the last evidence in the Prosecution case where Mr. Stojic talked about a "final military solution" to what he considered or to what was considered the "Muslim problem." "The strategy," and this is coming from Exhibits -- Exhibits all reporting on this same meeting, P 03530, P 03545, P 03547. And it's reported: "The strategy is to take over East Mostar through an HVO/HV offensive from the south. To facilitate this military offensive Bruno Stojic is proposing that UNPROFOR to evacuate the entire Muslim civilian population from East Mostar." It was during this time on the 17th of July, 1993, that Stojic said: "It may take 20 more days but at the end of it it will be either us or them." And that's reflected in Exhibits, again, the ones I just referred to, also Exhibit P 10367, and the testimony of Witness DZ. In his statement, again which was admitted as Exhibit P 09078, Jadranko Prlic said that the first expulsion of Muslims happened just after 9 May 1993. The second time that Prlic received information about the expulsion of Muslims he said was in July 1993, after which he says he offered his resignation to Mate Boban because he, that is Prlic, was against the expulsion of citizens of Muslim ethnic origin. That's at his statement, transcript pages 124 to 126. It is interesting that this was around the same time as Bruno Stojic's statements about resolving the Muslim problem once and for all in Mostar. Prlic said he offered his resignation because -- excuse me, no goals of fighting of any nation or any person could justify the behaviour or the actions that were taking place in Mostar. Referring to information that Mr. Praljak has provided to us in the course of the trial, he confirmed in fact that Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, or Rama as he calls it, using the Croatian word, cannot be separated, that is Vakuf and Prozor, and that in Prozor "things happened there such as the expulsion of Muslims." And that can be found in the transcript at page 22249 to 22250. I want to turn now for a few minutes to more about the operation of the HVO prisons and detention camps. And for purposes of these submissions, Your Honours, the part that I'm going to focus on is not so much what happened in 1993, although that again will be covered largely in the submissions concerning Mr. Coric and Mr. Pusic, but I think it's important and helpful for the Trial Chamber to recall the evidence of the establishment and operation of these camps in 1992, for indeed these HVO camps and prisons had been not just of recent vintage, they had already been administered and used in one war, that is with the Serbs in 1992. Indeed, again, in his statement P 09078, Jadranko Prlic indicated that the HVO detention centres were established and formed during the war with the JNA in 1992. One of the many important documents in this respect is Exhibit P 00292, which is the decree on the treatment of persons captured in armed fighting in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, dated 1 September 1992. The Chamber may recall testimony about this document and the document itself which states at Article 2: "The head of the justice and administration department, in cooperation with the head of the defence department and the head of the department of interior, shall designate the locations where prisoners shall be kept in accordance with the provisions of the aforementioned convention in Article 1 of this decree." Article 3 of the same document says: "The defence department shall be in charge of the facilities stipulated in Article 2 of this decree." And indeed Exhibit P 00452 is -- is the decision issued by Bruno Stojic as head of the HVO defence department establishing the central prison at the Heliodrom in September of 1992. From the moment that he was appointed chief of the military police administration in April 1992, Valentin Coric took an active part in establishing and administering HVO prisons or prison camps including the Heliodrom, which Mr. Coric also directly participated in setting up in September 1992. In fact, it was his recommendation that had gone to Mr. Stojic, and you can find that in Exhibit P 00513, also Exhibit P 00515. Exhibit P 00916 is an order dated the 16th of December, 1992, from the commander of the 3rd Company, 3rd Battalion, HVO Military Police, indicating that the HVO Military Police, under the command of Valentin Coric, was in charge of the Heliodrom in that particular order, ordering that all detainees must be referred to the Heliodrom military prison. As I mentioned earlier this afternoon, Exhibit P 00956 provides a very good overview and summary in connection with the operations of the military police from April through December 1992, including the establishment of the various HVO prisons and camps. It is Valentin Coric's own report over his name and provides extensive information for the Chamber's consideration. Let me just pick out a few of the items that the Chamber may wish to review. In that report, first of all, it indicates that on the 13th of April, by a decision of the president of the HZ HB, that is Mr. Boban, Mr. Valentin Coric was indeed, this is in the report itself, his report, was appointed assistant commander of the security and information service and all existing military police units were placed under his, that is, Coric's command. The document also informs us that at this time a military investigation prison in Capljina was established, the fourth in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. However, the military police administration attempted to establish a central military prison because the existing military investigation prisons had poorly appointed premises and were not able to receive the required number of prisoners of war. It goes on to say: "In early September by the decision of the defence department, the central military prison was established in Mostar." And again going full circle back to the orders by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Coric to establish the Heliodrom. It then goes on in a specific section of this long report on the military police, and there's a section titled "Detainees and prisoners." "By the end of June 1992, due to the needs of the HZ HB, the military administration established three military investigation prisons in Ljubuski, Mostar, and Livno. All prisoners of war and detainees, HVO soldiers who have committed a misdemeanour or an offence, and civilians who have committed a misdemeanour or an offence against HVO members were placed in them." It goes on to talk about, again, the establishment of the central military prison in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Scott kindly slow down again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. In that report, and I'm skipping over certain provisions because of time, but specifically it is mentioned the treatment of prisoners and prison conditions are in accordance with international conventions as confirmed by the representatives of the International Organisation for Human Rights Protection, the Helsinki Watch, during their visit on 24 October 1992. Long before 1993 prisons were being operated, international standards were being discussed, inspections were taking place. Mr. Coric's report goes on to say: "The military police is involved in the exchange of prisoners of war through its representatives on negotiating committees for exchanges and in conducting actual exchanges. In the military police administration, the necessary records are kept on our imprisoned defenders and the prisoners of war from the enemy side." The -- on the report on the detainees in the prisons it ends with this statement, which, again, I think the Chamber should consider in terms of what happens in 1993: "The military police has also set up required cooperation with municipal organs as well as with international organisations and institutions, ICRC, ECMM, UNPROFOR." Exhibit P 00677 is another important document. It is a report again from Valentin Coric as chief of the military police reporting to Bruno Stojic, his superior, as head of the HVO department of defence, dated 31 October 1992. Among other things, this document again shows that the HVO's Livno, Mostar, and Tomislavgrad prisons were under HVO military police administration. Again, indicating Coric reporting to Stojic. I invite Your Honours to take a close look at that report and listen to it and thinking -- this is a report that's been given in October 1992, not October 1993, but it might sound very similar, but this is during the time when primarily Serbs were being held, not Muslims. In that report Mr. Coric says: "Pursuant to an agreement reached with the ICRC, EU observers, and UNPROFOR, and the order issued by the chief of the defence department on the 28th of October 1992, all war prisoners were unconditionally released from the military remand centres in Livno, Mostar, and Tomislavgrad on 30 October 1992. The ICRC representatives have carried out a survey among incarcerated prisoners in which they express their preference about whether or not they wish to go to so-called Yugoslavia." It goes on at length about that, where certain prisoners wanted to go, didn't want to go in conjunction with the EU and ICRC representatives. It goes on to say: "So on 30 October 1992, the order to release prisoners from the military remand centres in Livno, Mostar, and Tomislavgrad were carried out. In all, 363 prisoners have been released in the presence of ICRC and EU representatives." Exhibit P 00740 is an HVO security and information service, what the Chamber has heard referred to as SIS, a report dated the 13th of November, 1992, concerning prisoners taken from the Heliodrom for labour at various HVO locations, including at the front lines. In this report, November 1992, the deputy warden at the Heliodrom, Josip Praljak, confirmed that they had recorded every instance when prisoners were taken out to work. The document goes on to say: "Up until 27 October 1992, the process of taking out prisoners to work involved certification of the request by one of the individuals in charge of logistics and verbal notification of Valentin Coric, chief of the HZ HB military police administration. According to the sources," I'm still quoting from the document, "according to the sources, they complained about this manner of taking out prisoners as a result of which Valentin Coric issued a decision announcing that no one was allowed to take out prisoners without his signature." Now, taking that bit of evidence about the camps in 1992, we can connect that to again referring back to Dr. Miller's report on the characteristics of the Balkan conflict, and that again is Exhibit P 10239 at page 15. And once again Dr. Miller reports that already by mid-1992, "the widespread existence of detention camps, which serve also as places of organised killing and organised rape, was a known phenomenon." "Regarding the infamous camps that dotted Bosnia during the war, one of the best known Manjaca, near Banja Luka, had been used as a prisoner of war camp during the first year of the war in Croatia." Then he goes on to refer to: "In July 1992, Red Cross representatives visited camps and prisons in Mostar, Ljubuski, Capljina, Bosanski Brod, Zenica, and Bjelica ..." "And in that year -- and in the year since the conflict began violations of humanitarian and human rights have been committed by all sides in the conflict and have become a practice, particularly as far as the civilian population is concerned. By August 1992," I'm still referring to Dr. Miller's report. "By August 1992, the existence of HVO camps at Ljubuski and Capljina were known as were the Serbian camps as well." Finally on this before a couple of final comments on the camps, again we have the assistance of Mr. Praljak who has indicated that he had authority over the HVO prison camps or at least the Dretelj camp in 1992 during the time that Serbs were being detained there. According to what Mr. Praljak has told us at transcript page 1624, it was Mr. Praljak who closed the Dretelj camp in 1992. I will just make reference to the fourth report of the UN Special Rapporteur Mazowiecki, his fourth report which is in evidence, it is Exhibit P 04822, and it goes on at great length at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like it -- the record to read Josip Praljak so that when reading the record people don't think that that is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm specifically referring to Slobodan Praljak. At transcript page 1624, Mr. Slobodan Praljak told us in court that he was the one who closed Dretelj camp in 1992. But I'm sure we can refer to the transcript and check that. Perhaps Mr. Praljak forgot. Your Honour, in the fourth report by Mr. Mazowiecki, it goes on at length about the operation of the camps, and I think when the Chamber has a chance to read that about Heliodrom, Dretelj, Gabela, you will see that it dovetails completely with the first-hand evidence that the Chamber received from a number of people who were held in these terrible camps and the UN special report confirms that. The point, Your Honour, that the Prosecution makes in this particular part of its submission and the Chamber may say, well, why talk about 1992, because, Your Honour, the establishment and operation of the camps was nothing new in 1993, and when there was the mass arrests of Muslim men in the early July 1993, they had to put them somewhere. They had been in the business of operating camps in 1992. They had been in the business of having international observers in the camps in 1992, and they knew the standards that were required. They'd been down this road before. Just briefly on forced labour. Again we've already touched on that only briefly, but the record indicates in this case, Your Honour, that this was a widespread and systematic practice. Again it couldn't be more systematic. Books and records of the prisoners being taken on a daily basis for forced labour, some of them not coming back because they were killed on the confrontation line. Just two quick examples on that. Exhibit P 03474. On the 15th of July, 1993, Mr. Petkovic ordered HVO units throughout the south-east Herzegovina operative zone to "organise immediately the fortification and barricading of defence lines reached and at depth in the zone by engaging engineering equipment, prisoners, and detainees." And a few days later, on the 20th of July, 1993, in Exhibit P 03592, Petkovic ordered again in connection with the engineering of defence works, "Engage the prisoners and available machinery in the completion of this task." I want to spend, Your Honour, a couple of minutes talking about what's been referred to in this case as reverse ethnic cleansing and the Prosecution submits this is particularly interesting and important because it truly shows the systematic nature and deliberateness of this plan, a plan and a strategy that involve not all -- ultimately not only involving Muslims but involving moving Bosnian Croats also. Indeed in a scheme in which Witness BF in one of his reports that the Chamber is familiar with described this practice as being truly Machiavellian. By a number of means Croats from other parts of Bosnia were prodded or "encouraged to leave their homes in order to establish or consolidate a Croatian population majority in the municipalities more at the core of the Banovina and Herceg-Bosna." The Prosecution submits that this part of the Greater Croatia-Herceg-Bosna programme had at least three important goals. First, it was clear to probably anyone who looked at it with any sort of intellectual objectivity that some municipalities and areas claimed by Herceg-Bosna were more Croat than others and with some of the areas on the fringes more toward the east, more towards Central Bosnia not having a strong Croat majority or even plurality. A judgement was made, we submit, or evolved over time that it was ultimately more important to Herceg-Bosna's long-term success to move the Croat population from the more marginal areas or on the edges, if you will, to the core areas where the Croat majority could thereby -- which could thereby be reinforced or consolidated. Tudjman himself recognised the benefits to be gained from moving Croats out of their homes even though difficult. In Exhibit P 06485, Tudjman says: "Of course it is painful. Apart from that, 200.000 Croats have already been driven out of their areas. There will probably be another 100.000 of them. It is awful for them, but even looked at historically, you know, we shall have these 100.000 to 200.000 Croats will firm up the Croatian territory here from Istria to Baranja, you understand, when we finish that and so on. So every bad thing is not just bad, but we have to make use of it here." As a second reason, as a matter of political, military, and economic practicalities and part of the ultimate what I will call horse trading with the Serbs and the Muslims, Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna leaders recognised that they might have to give up or trade away some of the areas furthest from the core Banovina territory. Perhaps the best example of that, Your Honours, is Vares, the eastern-most territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna, virtually surrounded by Serb and Muslim areas. Third and equally important and as already mentioned, relocating Croats from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and moving them into houses and flats which had been seized from or abandoned by Muslim families or Muslim families which have been expelled would make it more difficult, if not impossible, for the Muslims to return to those areas, their houses having been taken over by Croats. Once again Tudjman said in September 1993, and this is in Exhibit 52 -- 5255: "I, too, have told our people, please settle these refugees in those areas, Tasovcici, Stolac et cetera, to be Croats, so that Croatian people are present there." At the same meeting Tudjman told his Herzegovinian followers not to fall prey to the idea that the left bank of the Neretva River would become part of the Bosnian republic but do the opposite and to quote Tudjman "settle in those areas Ravno, Capljina, Neum, Stolac, and then we shall insist on it." In addition to the internal record that we have of HVO documents and presidential meetings, we also have the observations of the international observers. Representatives of the international organisations such as Witness BA and Witness DZ testified how the issue of population transfers of large groups of Bosnian Croat displaced persons was a recurring topic of conversation with the HVO leadership from at least mid-1993 forward, including specifically conversations and meetings with Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, and others who requested international organisations to assist in what was being called the "evacuation" of tens of thousands of Bosnian Croats from Central Bosnia into the Herzegovina region. That can be seen in part in Exhibit P 09712, P 02714, P 02872. Referring more to Witness BA who knew from colleagues in Central Bosnia that most of the Croats in Zenica were not in fact experiencing serious problems, at least not as reported to the international community, even though there was an ongoing armed conflict, they were confirmed that these people, most of them, did not in fact want to move from that area. In general, it was the policy of that organisation, the humanitarian organisation of which Witness BA was a part, to assist in evacuations only in situations where civilians were seriously at risk, and it was the assessment of that organisation that that was not the case concerning the Croats in the Zenica area. Likewise, Witness BC interviewed Bosnian Croat displaced persons who spoke about the circumstances of their departure, and many of them reported to Witness BC that they were manipulated or coerced by HVO soldiers into getting onto buses. Many of them didn't want to leave he told us. The typical modus operandi would be the soldiers would come into the village, say something to the effect, We're withdrawing from this area. The Mujahedin are on the way, and you better leave while you can. Many of the Bosnian Croats in fact were very angry later because they didn't want to leave their homes and didn't feel that they really needed to, but nonetheless were given no choice. The use of fear, as I just mentioned, was often combined with the promises of better housing or better conditions somewhere else in Herzegovina or elsewhere, which unfortunately often didn't turn out to be the case for the Croat displaced persons themselves, who indeed were also victims of this programming strategy. Not just the Muslims but Bosnian Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, just one small precision. What you've just told us, how is this compatible with what happened in Guca Gora where the Mujahedin in fact did come?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, the evidence on that was not quite so clear, because I think the testimony of the witness was that the situation in Guca Gora, while there had been some very bad things happen there, were not accurately reported. But be that as it may, again let me be very clear about the Prosecution position, we have said since the opening statement in this case that there were indeed times when there were crimes and atrocities committed by the Muslim side and there indeed were some instances of that. There's no question about that. But what the witnesses in this case have established, we submit, over and over again, and what the international documents show, is that apart from that, apart from some genuine instances that there was a plan, strategy, a manipulation to move many -- by the Bosnian Croat leadership to move many Bosnian Croats from Central Bosnia to Herzegovina and we believe, we submit, that's what the evidence shows. Witness BA -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was going on when you asked your question. I think we covered that already. Witness Peter Galbraith testified how Mate Boban, in July 1993, told him that the HVO and Croatia wanted to move a large number of Croats from the Vares area to Croat-controlled areas, presumably Herzegovina. What Galbraith thought was striking, what he told us in court, what he thought was striking was that Boban did not seek international assistance to protect the Croat population in place, that is leave them in Vares and protect them there, but what Boban wanted to do was to move them out of Vares. We also have the report and the written account of Witness DE, which is Exhibit P 080865 -- I think there's a mistake in that by the numbers. Your Honour, I'll have to double-check it. That's too many numbers. It may be P 0 -- I'll have to check on that, Your Honour, my apologies. But in the written account in connection with Witness DE he said this and I think he encapsulated it as clearly as anyone did: "I accuse the highest level of Croatian politics of betraying Croatian interest in Central Bosnia, especially in Vares where I was born. Many things are now clear about the fall of both Travnik and Kakanj. It was all done according to a premeditated scenario. I accuse them of unprecedented exodus of the Croats from Vares, of their suffering and ordeal. You have done everything to drive us out of our centuries' old homes. What is the area you have allocated to us for our future life?" I'm told it is P 08086. And I'll finally return to this where I started on this topic, and that is the ECMM report dated the 19th of July, 1993, which is Exhibit P 02849 that was authored by Witness BF who testified recently. He gave the following striking and I think evocative assessment of this situation: "It seems Machiavellic, but it is only Balkan. And everybody who has met regularly the top Bosnian Croat leaders Boban, Stojic, Kordic, Valenta, in various situations and on various subjects where their paranoia and their extremism was not hidden can easily believe it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake on line 20 -- oh, it's corrected now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Coming to the end of this overview, Your Honour, we're now into the fall of 1993. Not surprisingly, the continued illegal forced transfer and imprisonment of civilians led the international community to place increasingly great pressure on both Croatia and on the Herceg-Bosna leadership. As a result, on the 6th of September, 1993, the HVO cabinet or government held a special meeting to deal with these problems having become alarmed again at the political and public relations damage being done both locally and in Zagreb, and this can be found in Exhibit P 04841. After trying to pretend that the HVO cabinet was not responsible for the human rights violations in the very camps that they had established, enlarged and administered, they arranged for a few limited improvements but made no immediate efforts to close the camps. The camps, after all, still had a reason to exist as long as Muslims remained in them. Only when most of the Muslims had already been expelled or moved to other locations were camps, or most of them, closed at the end of 1993, although some in fact were not closed until 1994. The Herceg-Bosna HVO campaign of attacks and ethnic cleansing carried out by the HVO military under direction of the Herceg-Bosna political leaders continued into the latter part of 1993 as demonstrated once again by the 23 October 1993 attack on the Muslim village of Stupni Do. I'm not going to, for these purposes, go into detail on that particular event, but I think the Chamber has heard extensive evidence about that and rather compelling evidence from -- including people on the HVO side. After discussions in Zagreb of what to do concerning the HVO officer who the Chamber will know, who commanded the Herceg-Bosna forces involved in the killings at Stupni Do, senior political and military leaders engaged in what Franjo Tudjman himself described as a "game." The Chamber has heard about all the efforts to conceal and cover up the crimes committed under the leadership order of Ivica Rajic. The giving of a false name; how Ivica Rajic became Viktor Andric. How he was supposedly fired and the new person Viktor Andric put in his place. It was one and the same person as Ivica Rajic. All the manoeuvering that went on and truly what must have been one of the biggest cover-ups of the Balkan wars. And what Tudjman himself described and there are several presidential meetings where Stupni Do, it was discussed at length and in fact Mr. Petkovic participates in some of these meetings, and Mr. Tudjman's own word for what was being done was to call it a game. The international community was told in fact that Rajic had been removed when in fact he had changed his name, remained in essentially the same position. And the very troops that went into Stupni Do, they then turned around days later and used -- attempt to break through from Kiseljak to Busovaca. The very breakthrough that Tudjman said on the 5th of November, gave instructions to Petkovic and said, Push on to Busovaca. In the Resolution adopted on 20 December 1993, the General Assembly condemned the indiscriminate shelling of civilians and murder of non-combatants, specifically singling out the Bosnian Croats. The ethnic cleansing perpetrated by any side, particularly the Bosnian Serb forces who have used such tactics as a matter of policy and Bosnian Croat forces. Once again in the same Security Council or in this instance General Assembly action, and that can be found at P 07268, the General Assembly once again urged the government of Croatia to use its influence "with the self-proclaimed Croatian authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina to bring the practice of ethnic cleansing to an immediate end and to reverse the effects of that practice." The sixth report of Mazowiecki, the Special Rapporteur appointed by the UN, the sixth report which is Exhibit P 07917, once again provides a lengthy report and factual statement of what had happened in Herzegovina during this time period. I won't take the time now to read the quote from it. The Chamber will have it. As a result of the Herceg-Bosna HVO campaign of persecution and ethnic cleansing, the Bosnian Muslim population in many parts of Herceg-Bosna was substantially reduced and likewise the Bosnian Croat percentage of the population was substantially increased. Those Muslims who remained were plainly dominated by the Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities and forces as planned and intended, indeed, by the joint criminal enterprise. By the late fall of 1993, the cleansing of Muslims from many parts of Herceg-Bosna was largely completed, and there was little continuing need for the camps. While in September, just in September of 1993, there had still been 8.000 Muslims in Stolac and 14.000 Muslims in Capljina, by November only one month later, by November there were no Muslims left in Stolac, and out of 14.000 that had been in Capljina the month before, there were only 3.852 left. The full extent of -- and the success of their efforts to move the Muslims out was clearly known to the HVO leadership. In one meeting, the convicted war criminal and Bosnian Croat vice-president Dario Kordic reported that "about 75.000 Muslims have been expelled by the HV." Maybe that's a typo. Maybe it should be the HVO. We want to give them the benefit of the doubt, but that can be found in Exhibit P 08597. About 75.000 Muslims have been expelled. Zoran Maric bragged to Tudjman, bragged to Tudjman in a meeting already in March 1993, at the moment there are very few Muslims in Busovaca. Many wish to return, but "we put Croats in their homes." That's Exhibit P 01622. In a remarkable meeting on 21 September 1993, which is Exhibit P 05237, the HVO's Andjelko Markovic proudly informed Tudjman: "Today there is not a single Muslim in Stolac. We have populated Stolac with our refugees from Bosnia." Tudjman responded: "Andjelko, I know all that. You're not telling me anything I don't already know." Pero Markovic of the Capljina HVO reported to Tudjman, another Markovic, in the same meeting: "When it comes to the territory south of the Buna down to Stolac and back to Capljina, this is an area of approximately 250 kilometres square, there is not a single Muslim there. Croats live there, and we have brought 3.000 Croats from Kakanj, from Travnik, too, and Croats from Konjic. All the houses that are sound are full. There are priests that followed in their steps too." "Tudjman: Wait. I said that the containers too, and that too. "Markovic: We have about a hundred cottages. We have already filled the Stolac area to capacity." Tudjman said he had given instructions for Croats to settle in these areas. I actually quoted that earlier. "I, too, have told our people, please settle these refugees in those areas so Croatian people are there." Exhibit P 05237. The work of the Prosecution witness Dr. Tabeau showed the following based on what she described as statistically conservative analysis. She studied the population movements in eight of the Herceg-Bosna municipalities and among her conclusions were the following: The studied Herceg-Bosna population became divided along ethnic lines during the 1993 Croat-Muslim conflict. Probably wouldn't surprise any of us. Going on though, approximately 43.2 per cent of the pre-conflict population of non-Croats in eight Herceg-Bosna municipalities were not living at their 1991 place of residence by 1997, 1998. 43.2 per cent had been displaced. 49 per cent of the pre-conflict population of Muslims in the eight Herceg-Bosna municipalities were not living at their 1991 residences in 1997 -- by 1997, 1998, specifically Muslims. 49 per cent. While each ethnic group suffered, and again the Prosecution will always say all groups suffered, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, while each ethnic group suffered, the highest number of internally displaced persons and refugees were the Bosnian Muslims, a minimum, again being statistically conservative, a minimum of 26.663 to 40.266 internally displaced persons or refugees or 43.4 per cent of the total of all internally displaced persons and refugees were Muslims. Looking at some of the areas covered by our indictment, in comparison to the ethnic percentages between 1991 and 1997, 1998, Prozor went from being 62.2 per cent Croat to being 93 per cent Croat. Mostar-Jug went to from being 49 per cent Croat to 96.1 per cent Croat. Mostar-Jugozapad - forgive my pronunciation if I don't have it correct - went from being 47.9 per cent Croat to being 78.2 per cent Croat. Mostar-Zapad went from being 41.6 per cent Croat to 75.2 per cent Croat. Capljina went from being 53.8 per cent Croat to 92.3 per cent Croat. And Stolac, Stolac went from being 48 per cent Muslim in 1991 to being 95.5 per cent Croat after the conflict. Any Muslims who still remained after all of this active HVO cleansing or those who might return would have to change their national identities according to Tudjman. Tudjman told various Croat leaders, and this is in Exhibit P 08288, "Start working on it right now to get them to declare themselves Croats of the Muslim faith. Get down to it right now. We have no other choice." That, Your Honour, really brings us to the Washington Agreement in March of 1994, and the end of the principal period of the amended indictment. Even by -- even then, the plan was still going forward. Even then Tudjman was urging his soldiers on, not to give up on Herceg-Bosna, that Herceg-Bosna would always exist, would never go away. And I would just close with the words of Witness DZ, who the Chamber heard recently, who put in his report, which is Exhibit P 08167, that many of the Croats that he was -- that he was dealing with in the spring of 1994, before he left the area described Washington -- the Washington Agreement as nothing other than a dictated marriage for a better divorce. Mr. President, that concludes our overview of the case, and Mr. Stringer and I tomorrow would specifically address some additional arguments, submissions put forth by the Coric and Pusic Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You've used four hours roughly. I'm not going to count the number of missing seconds or minutes. Let's say that tomorrow you have four more hours. It would be good if you could complete your submissions tomorrow. Of course in our decision we had granted you nine hours, but you might be able to complete your submissions tomorrow. As you know, tomorrow we'll work in the morning at 9.00 a.m. So I'll see you tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.
